intro: People live together in homes, schools and towns. Many people learn ways to be kind and fair. Many learn these ways from their families and religions.
In this unit, you will hear the Golden Rule in many voices. You will see ways people give, pray, rest and say thank you. Some families do none of these, and that is fine too.
By the end, you will be able to name what different traditions do. You will know how to be kind when others do things in their own way.
bigQuestion: How do people in many traditions learn to be kind, fair and thankful?

timeline.t: Hear the Golden Rule: treat others as you want to be treated
Learn Hillel's and Jesus's words about treating others
Learn a saying of the Prophet Muhammad about caring
Hear what Confucius and the Buddha taught
See how people give: tzedakah, zakat, langar and charity
See ways families say thank you at meals and on Shabbat
See ways people pray and sing
Practice a quiet minute and being respectful

words.d: treat others the way you want to be treated
a Jewish word for giving to people in need
a gift Muslims give each year to help people in need
a free kitchen at a Sikh gurdwara where anyone can eat
the Jewish day of rest, from Friday evening to Saturday evening
the prayer Muslims say five times a day
sitting still and paying calm attention
treating people and their ways with care

test.q: Treat others the way you want to be treated. What is this called?
Which teacher was Jewish and lived long ago?
Who kept sayings of the Prophet Muhammad?

test.why: Langar is at the Sikh gurdwara.

test.q: When do many Jewish families light Shabbat candles?
What do many Muslims kneel on to pray?
test.why: Muslims often pray on a rug.

test.q: A friend's family does not pray. What is true?
choices: That is fine; every family has its own way.
test.why: Some families do not pray, and they are welcome too.

choices: Do not do to others what you do not want.
test.why: Confucius taught not to do to others what you do not want done to you.

write.prompt: Pick two voices from this unit, like Hillel and Confucius. Draw or tell how each one says to treat others. How are they alike?
tips: Say which people keep the words: "Muslims remember..."
Tell how the words are alike.
Use a unit word, like Golden Rule.

title: Being Kind, Being Fair

chapters.title: Golden Rules
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do so many traditions teach people to treat others well?

story.title: The Forgotten Lunch
story.kicker: One child has no lunch, and six friends have an idea.
paragraphs: It is lunch time. Six friends sit at one long table. They open their lunch boxes. Sam looks in his bag. It is empty. He left his lunch at home.
Sam feels sad. His tummy is loud. Ava sees his face. She says, "You can have half my sandwich." Omar gives him some grapes. Priya gives him a cracker.
Soon Sam has a full lunch! Leo says, "My grandma says to treat people the way you want to be treated." Noor nods. "My family says that too," she says.
Each friend's family has words for this idea. The words sound a little different. But the idea is the same. Many people call it the Golden Rule.
story.think: How did the friends help Sam? How would you want to be treated if you forgot your lunch?

lessons.title: The Golden Rule
lessons.mainIdea: The Golden Rule says: treat others the way you want to be treated.
reading: Think about how you like to be treated. You like kind words. You like to be asked to play. You like fair turns.
The *Golden Rule* says to treat others that way too. People in many religions teach this rule. People with no religion teach it too.

words.d: treat others the way you want to be treated

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Look at the swing on the playground. Two children want it. One child says, "You go first. Then it is my turn." Both children smile.
look.prompt: How does this show the Golden Rule?

check.q: What does the Golden Rule say?
choices: Treat others the way you want to be treated.
Only be kind to your friends.
check.why: The Golden Rule asks us to treat others the way we want to be treated.

check.q: Who teaches the Golden Rule?
choices: People in many religions, and people with no religion
check.why: Many religions teach it, and people with no religion teach it too.

check.q: Which one follows the Golden Rule?
choices: Sharing the swing with a friend
check.why: Sharing is how we like to be treated, so it follows the Golden Rule.

lessons.title: Jesus and Hillel
lessons.mainIdea: Jesus and Hillel were Jewish teachers who taught the Golden Rule long ago.
reading: *Hillel* was a Jewish teacher long ago. A story says a man asked him to teach all of the Torah fast. Hillel said: do not do to others what you do not like. The rest explains it.
Jesus was a Jewish teacher too. Christians follow his teachings. The Bible says Jesus taught: do to others what you want them to do to you.

words.d: a famous Jewish teacher who lived about 2,000 years ago
the holy book of Christians

look.title: Words from the Bible
look.text: And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise.
look.prompt: These are old words. What do you think they mean in your own words?

check.q: Who was Hillel?
choices: A Jewish teacher from long ago
check.why: Hillel was a famous Jewish teacher.

check.q: Which book tells what Jesus taught?
check.why: Christians read about Jesus in the Bible.

check.q: What did Hillel say to the man?
choices: Do not do to others what you do not like.
check.why: The Talmud tells that Hillel said not to do to others what you would not like.

lessons.title: The Prophet Muhammad
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims remember that the Prophet Muhammad taught to want good for others.
reading: *Muslims* follow the religion of Islam. They honor the Prophet Muhammad. They keep sayings of his in books called hadith.
One saying teaches this. A person should want for a brother what he wants for himself. Muslims read it as a call to care for others.

words.d: people who follow the religion of Islam

look.title: A Saying of the Prophet
look.text: None of you truly believes until he wants for his brother what he wants for himself.
look.cite: Hadith 13 in al-Nawawi's Forty Hadith (from al-Bukhari and Muslim), in our own words
look.prompt: What does this saying ask a person to want?

check.q: What religion do Muslims follow?
check.why: Muslims follow the religion of Islam.

check.q: The saying asks a person to want good things for whom?
check.why: The hadith asks people to want for others what they want for themselves.

check.q: What are the hadith?
choices: Sayings of the Prophet Muhammad that Muslims keep
check.why: Muslims keep the Prophet's sayings in books called hadith.

lessons.title: Confucius and the Buddha
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius and the Buddha also taught people not to hurt others.
reading: *Confucius* was a teacher in China long ago. A student asked for one rule for all of life. Confucius said: what you do not want for yourself, do not do to others.
The Buddha was a teacher in India. Buddhists follow his teachings. A book called the Dhammapada says: everyone fears being hurt. So do not hurt others.

words.d: a teacher in China who lived about 2,500 years ago
a teacher in India whom Buddhists follow; the name means awake one

look.title: Words of Confucius
look.text: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
look.cite: Analects 15:23, in our own words (compare Legge's translation, 1861)
look.prompt: How is this like Hillel's words?

check.q: Where did Confucius teach?
check.why: Confucius was a teacher in China long ago.

check.q: Which book has sayings of the Buddha?
check.why: The Dhammapada is a book of the Buddha's sayings.

check.q: What did the Buddha teach about hurting?
choices: Hurting is fine if you win.
Everyone fears being hurt, so do not hurt others.
check.why: The Dhammapada teaches that all fear harm, so we should not harm others.

lessons.title: Giving to People in Need
lessons.mainIdea: Many religions teach giving to people who need help.
reading: Jews call giving *tzedakah*. It means doing what is right. Many Jewish families keep a small box for coins to give.
Muslims give *zakat*. Each year, Muslims who have enough give a small part of their savings to people in need. Christians often call giving charity.

words.d: a Jewish word for giving to people in need; it means doing what is right
a gift Muslims give each year to help people in need

look.title: A Common Zakat Rule
look.cite: The common rule: 2.5 out of every 100 in savings each year
look.prompt: Out of 100 coins, how many are given? Is it a big part or a small part?

check.q: What is tzedakah?
choices: A Jewish word for giving to those in need
check.why: Tzedakah is Jewish giving; it means doing what is right.

check.q: Who gives zakat?
check.why: Zakat is giving in Islam.

check.q: What do many Jewish families keep for giving?
check.why: Many Jewish families keep a tzedakah box.

lessons.title: Langar: A Meal for All
lessons.mainIdea: At a Sikh langar, everyone sits and eats together for free.
reading: Sikhs follow Guru Nanak. He taught that all people are equal. Sikh stories tell how he shared his food with the hungry.
At every gurdwara there is a free kitchen called *langar*. Anyone may come and eat. Rich and poor sit side by side. Helpers cook and serve.

words.d: a free kitchen at a Sikh gurdwara where anyone can eat
a Sikh house of worship

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Look at the long rows of people on the floor. A grandma sits next to a boy. A doctor sits next to a bus driver. Helpers bring warm bread and soup to each one.
look.prompt: Why do you think everyone sits together at langar?

check.q: Where is langar served?
check.why: Langar is the free kitchen at a Sikh gurdwara.

check.q: Who may eat at langar?
check.why: Langar is open to all people.

check.q: What did Guru Nanak teach?
check.why: Sikhs remember that Guru Nanak taught all people are equal.

review.q: Which words match the Golden Rule?
choices: Treat others the way you want to be treated.

review.q: Who was a Jewish teacher long ago?
Muslims give a yearly gift to people in need. What is it called?
A free Sikh kitchen for all is called what?
review.why: Langar is the Sikh free kitchen.

review.q: Why do people say the Golden Rule has many voices?
choices: It is a song with many singers.
Only one person ever said it.
Many traditions teach it in their own words.
review.why: Many traditions teach the same idea in different words.

chapters.title: Quiet Time and Thank-You Time
chapters.bigQuestion: What are some ways people are quiet or say thank you?

story.title: One Minute of Quiet
story.kicker: The teacher rings a soft bell, and the room gets still.
paragraphs: Ms. Ruiz rings a soft bell. "Now we have one minute of quiet," she says. "You may use it any way that helps you feel calm."
Ben closes his eyes. He breathes in slowly and out slowly. Grace folds her hands. She says a silent prayer. Ali looks out the window at a tree.
Rosa hums a song in her head. Dev just sits still and rests. Nobody talks. Nobody laughs at anyone. Everyone lets the others be.
The bell rings again. "How do you feel?" asks Ms. Ruiz. "Calm," says Ben. "Ready," says Dev. Each child used the quiet in their own way.
story.think: What did each child do with the quiet minute? What helps you feel calm?

lessons.title: Thanks Before a Meal
lessons.mainIdea: Many families say thank you before or after they eat.
reading: Look at a family at dinner. Before they eat, some Christian families hold hands. They say a short prayer called *grace*. It thanks God for the food.
Jewish families say blessings over bread and after meals. Muslims often say bismillah, in the name of God, before eating. Some families just say thanks to the cook.

words.d: a short prayer of thanks said before or after a meal

look.title: Words from the Torah
look.text: When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee.
look.prompt: When does this verse say to give thanks?

check.q: What is grace?
choices: A short prayer of thanks at a meal
check.why: Grace is a prayer of thanks said at a meal.

check.q: Who often says bismillah before eating?
check.why: Many Muslims say bismillah, in the name of God, before eating.

check.q: Deuteronomy 8:10 says to give thanks when?
check.why: The verse says to bless God after eating and being full.

lessons.title: Candles on Friday Night
lessons.mainIdea: Many Jewish families light candles and say a blessing to start Shabbat.
reading: It is Friday. The sun is going down. In many Jewish homes, someone lights two candles. They say a *blessing*, words that thank God.
This starts *Shabbat*, the day of rest. It lasts until Saturday night. Families eat, sing, and rest together.

words.d: words that thank God or ask for good
the Jewish day of rest, from Friday evening to Saturday evening

look.title: A Week and Its Rest Day
look.cite: The Jewish calendar week; see Exodus 20:8-11
look.prompt: How many days come before Shabbat?

check.q: When does Shabbat start?
check.why: Shabbat starts at sundown on Friday.

check.q: What do many families light to start Shabbat?
check.why: Many Jewish families light two candles.

check.q: What is Shabbat?
check.why: Shabbat is the Jewish day of rest.

lessons.title: Five Prayers a Day
lessons.mainIdea: Many Muslims pray five times each day, facing toward Mecca.
reading: Look at the small rug on the floor. A Muslim man stands on it. He bows. Then he kneels and touches his forehead to the rug.
This prayer is called *salat*. Muslims pray it five times a day. They face toward Mecca, a holy city. A rug keeps the place clean.

words.d: the prayer Muslims say five times a day
a holy city in Saudi Arabia that Muslims face when they pray

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Dawn. Noon. Afternoon. Sunset. Night. Five times the prayer rug comes out. Five times it is rolled up again.
look.prompt: Count the times. Why might a rug help at each one?

check.q: How many times a day do many Muslims pray salat?
check.why: Salat is prayed five times each day.

check.q: Which way do Muslims face to pray?
check.why: Muslims face toward Mecca.

check.q: What is salat?
check.why: Salat is the Muslim prayer.

lessons.title: A Song of Praise
lessons.mainIdea: Many people sing to give thanks and to pray.
reading: Listen. In a church, people sing hymns. A *hymn* is a song of praise to God. In a Hindu temple, people sing as a lamp is waved.
At a gurdwara, Sikhs sing words from their holy book. Songs help many people feel close to God and to each other.

words.d: a song of praise, often sung in church

look.title: A Song from the Psalms
look.text: O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
look.prompt: What does this song ask people to do?

check.q: What is a hymn?
check.why: A hymn is a song of praise.

check.q: Where do Sikhs sing words from their holy book?
check.why: Sikhs sing at the gurdwara.

check.q: Psalm 136:1 asks people to do what?
check.why: The psalm says, give thanks unto the Lord.

lessons.title: Sitting and Breathing
lessons.mainIdea: Many Buddhists sit still and pay attention to their breath.
reading: Look at a woman sitting on a cushion. Her back is tall. Her eyes are soft. She feels her breath go in and out.
This is *meditation*. Many Buddhists meditate to calm the mind. Many other people sit and breathe quietly too.

words.d: sitting still and paying calm attention, like to your breath

look.title: Try It
look.text: Sit tall. Put one hand on your tummy. Breathe in slowly. Feel your hand rise. Breathe out slowly. Feel it fall. Do this three times.
look.prompt: How did your body feel after three slow breaths?

check.q: What is meditation?
check.why: Meditation means sitting still and paying calm attention.

check.q: Who often meditates to calm the mind?
check.why: Meditation is a key Buddhist practice.

check.q: What does the woman pay attention to?
check.why: She feels her breath go in and out.

lessons.title: Being Kind When Others Are Quiet
lessons.mainIdea: We stay calm and kind when someone else is praying or being quiet.
reading: Some families pray. Some sit in silence. Some do none of these things. Every family is *welcome* to its own way.
When someone is quiet or praying, we can help. We use soft voices. We wait. We do not laugh. This is being *respectful*.

words.d: treating people and their ways with care
glad to be included, just as you are

look.title: What Would You Do?
look.text: Your friend's grandpa is praying on his rug. You want to ask him a question. Your friend puts a finger to her lips.
look.prompt: What could you do while you wait?

check.q: Your friend is praying. What is respectful?
check.why: Waiting quietly is respectful.

check.q: Do all families pray?
check.why: Some families pray and some do not; all are welcome.

check.q: What does respectful mean?
choices: Treating people and their ways with care
check.why: Being respectful means treating others with care.

review.why: Shabbat is the Jewish day of rest.

review.q: Who prays salat five times a day?
A prayer of thanks at a meal is called what?
Sitting still and watching your breath is called what?

review.why: A hymn is a song of praise.

review.q: Someone near you is praying. What can you do?
choices: Use a soft voice and wait
review.why: Being quiet and waiting is respectful.
